Simulation-based passenger evacuation optimization in metro stations
considering multi-objectives
Kai Guo, Limao Zhang *
School of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Nanyang Technological University, 50 Nanyang Avenue, 639798, Singapore
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Emergency evacuation
Metro stations
Pedestrian behaviors
Evacuation prediction
Multi-objective optimization
A B S T R A C T
Evacuation is critical for safety management due to the highly overcrowded passengers in the metro stations. A
simulation-based approach integrating Random Forest (RF) and Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm III
(NSGA-III) is proposed to perform the evacuation evaluation and optimization at metro stations. A 3D model of
the metro station is built to simulate the dynamic process of passenger evacuation in metro stations. A framework
consisting of 9 influential factors and 3 objectives is developed to model the input-output relationship in pas­
senger evacuation. An RF-based meta-model is used to construct the relationship between influential factors and
objectives. At last, NSGA-III is applied to seeking the optimal solutions for the station renovation in order to
achieve a safe evacuation. A station model simulating a real metro station in Singapore is constructed to test the
effectiveness and applicability of the proposed approach. It is found that (1) A safe evacuation could be achieved
for the station, but along with the increasing passenger volume and panic level, the requirement of evacuation
objectives, the evacuation time and density, may not be met. Especially under the high passenger volume
conditions, the passenger density could reach up to 6.2 unit/m2 (extremely dangerous); (2) An average
improvement degree, 7.5%, can be achieved for the optimization of 20 test cases, and a maximum improvement
degree, 22.5%, can be achieved for the evacuation optimization at metro stations; (3) It could be difficult to keep
both of the evacuation time and density within the standards if one major exit is closed, even after the opti­
mization. But a larger average improvement degree, 10.8%, can be achieved by the proposed optimization
approach, which indicates the optimal solutions still could reduce the risk to a great extent. The novelty of this
research lies in that (a) An RF algorithm is incorporated to build the meta-model that can properly represent the
relationship between influential factors and objectives, despite the complexity and even conflicting between
them; (b) Optimal measures for the evacuation improvement are provided from the MOO perspective by inte­
grating NSGA-III. This hybrid approach can be used as a decision tool to assist regulatory authorities in devel­
oping effective emergency evacuation evaluation and optimization plans with adequate consideration of the
complexity and multi-objective nature under evacuation events.
1. Introduction
The metro system has become an indispensable part of the trans­
portation system for cities worldwide. Due to its energy efficiency,
environment friendly, free of traffic jams, convenience, and fast fea­
tures, it is becoming more and more favored by people. With a contin­
uous increase of rail traffic passenger volume, much more attention
must be paid to the safety and security in rail transit system operation,
since incidents occur frequently in metro stations worldwide, endan­
gering the safety and security of the metro operation. Given various
kinds of accidents occur during the evacuation of crowds in mass
gatherings, serious consequences have been made. Caused by the heavy
downpour and a fire accident between Raffles Place and Marina Bay, the
tunnels between Bishan and Braddell were seriously flooded on 7
October 2017 in Singapore [19]. Also in Singapore, two trains crashed at
the Joo Koon station on 15 November 2017, leading to 36 passengers
and 2 staff being injured [27]. As far as emergency officials concern, the
most important thing after the incident is to evacuate people from
dangerous places to safe areas. Evacuating people as quickly and safely
as possible can greatly reduce casualty and economic losses.
Studies on the safety improvement of emergency evacuation at metro
stations have become urgent concerns from both the practice and

research areas. An effective evacuation is very important to protect
passengers' safety and respond to emergencies. Researchers have put a
lot of efforts into the investigation of improving the evacuation at metro
stations. For example, in the study of Wang, et al. [67], a model of metro
stations was constructed to simulate the passenger evacuation process
under fire scenarios, aiming to evaluate the evacuation capacity of sta­
tions, identifying and analyzing the bottlenecks during the evacuation,
and providing suggestions on the evacuation strategies. Zhang, et al.
[73] developed a simulation-based multi-attribute decision approach to
perform the evacuation simulations for the analysis of evacuation route
choices, in which the evacuation route length, evacuation time, and
density were considered as the key performance indicators. Kallianiotis,
et al. [28] built simulation models to evaluate the evacuation capacity of
stations under the worst scenarios, and it was found that under critical
conditions, the passenger walking speed exerted the most significant
impact on the evacuation time. Mossberg, et al. [51] developed a virtual
reality model to study the potential of using elevators during the
emergency evacuation, where the impacts of different ways of guidance,
such as light guide and smart phone guide, were studied, and it was
found that smartphone guidance could increase the elevator usage and
improve the evacuation efficiency.
Many kinds of criteria, including the evacuation capacity, evacuation
time, and the maximum density, are proposed to measure the safety
level of evacuation events in most cases. For example, the competi­
tiveness of evacuees was studied as the main factor causing dangerous
clogs [15]. Information transmission (i.e., proper guide) was considered
as the most important factor that could guide evacuees to avoid collision
and find the exits effectively [21]. In the study of Han, et al. [22], the
utilization rate of exits, obstacles, and crowd decentralizing rate were
believed as the critical factors decisive for an effective evacuation. The
number and positions of leaders could exert a remarkable effect on the
evacuation, especially under the limited visibility scenarios [24]. More
importantly, not only the key influential factors could be disparate ac­
cording to different evacuation scenarios, but also it could be an
extremely complicated task to accurately build the relationship between
these factors and the desired objectives (criteria), due to the high un­
certainty and complexity in the evacuation events. As studies demon­
strated, automatic fare gates may allow occupants orderly to pass
through and avoid congestion but they seem to have little impact on the
effectiveness of the evacuation because of the unpredicted occupant
behavior [33]. The influence of the presence of obstacles during the
evacuation site could be elusive, as the obstacle was found beneficial for
improving the flow rate in some studies but unfavorable due to the
congestion and danger caused by it in other cases [35,42,75]. This
complexity between influential factors and objectives brings a great
challenge for the further investigation and optimization of safe
evacuation.
Conflicts commonly exist among different desired objectives for a
safe evacuation. A longer evacuation time and a higher density could
lead to evacuation risks [7,65]. However, the evacuation time and
density are related to each other in a very complex way. Reaching the
minimum should be ideal for both of them, but too much emphasis on
reducing the evacuation time (urge passengers to leave too quickly) may
cause a potential high-density risk, which raises the potential of risks,
such as stampede. Too much emphasis on reducing the density (guiding
passengers to evacuate at a slow and orderly pace) could lead to a longer
evacuation time and require more evacuation resources. Thus, the
improvement of evacuation should be considered as a multi-objective
optimization (MOO) problem. MOO especially refers to problems
where two or more objectives are desired to be optimized and a conflict
between the objectives exists at the same time. In seeking the optimal
evacuation plans, Yuan and Han [71] considered minimizing the evac­
uation time and the possible hazards related to the spaced-based
geographical conditions for improved safety during evacuation. Abdel­
ghany, et al. [1] presented a genetic algorithm (GA) based evacuation
optimization approach, where GA was used to search the optimal
evacuation plans for visitors under guidance, and the approach was
demonstrated to outperform conventional evacuation plans based on the
nearest-gate rule. However, it should be noticed that the current studies
on the MOO of evacuation problems mainly focused on relatively simple
scenarios, such as a hypothetical 10-mile evacuation network or the
single-story exhibition halls, or the route optimization was the major
task [1,26,72]. Actually, as reviewed, even though it would be much
more challenging, it is not only essential to investigate the evacuation
optimization in metro stations as a MOO problem, but also necessary to
consider complexity in it, such as small group behaviors, usher behav­
iors, and evacuation requirements under special incidents. However,
those complexities are rarely taken into account for evacuation
modeling, prediction, and optimization in the literature.
As introduced above, it could be a challenging task to properly
construct the relationship between the many influential factors for the
evacuation events. Especially, a complex and even conflicting relation­
ship could exist between the factors and objectives for the evacuation
problem at metro stations. To solve these problems, this research puts
efforts to answer the following questions: (1) How to identify the key
factors influencing the evacuation performance (objectives) of metro
stations and how to build the relationship between them; (2) How to
plan and optimize the evacuation with the consideration of the
complexity and conflicts in the evacuation events. To answer these two
questions, a hybrid approach in this research with the integration of
evacuation simulation tool, random forest (RF), and MOO algorithm is
built to find out the possible optimal solutions. This approach is ex­
pected to not only enrich the research of the evacuation events but also
fill the gap of few current studies investigating the complexity of and
potential optimization measures for the evacuation at metro stations
from the MOO perspective.
The rest of this research is presented as follows. In Section 2, a review
of emergency evacuation is presented. Section 3 explains the procedures
of the proposed approach in detail. A case is studied in Section 4 to
demonstrate the applicability of the proposed model, and discussions
are further made in Section 5. In Section 6, conclusions and future works
are drawn up.
2. Literature review on evacuation efficiency
Conducting emergency evacuation experiments in real-world con­
ditions could be too expensive and causing unexpected accidents or even
serious injuries. Simulation modeling has been proved to be one of the
most effective ways to study evacuation management and provide
evacuation improvement strategies. Evacuation simulation models
could be low-cost and harmless, which are especially great at replicating
real scenarios in the risk-free world [81]. Users could conduct evacua­
tion simulations of different scenarios, compare different strategies, gain
insights, and then determine the optimal solutions. Tweedie, et al. [64]
put an effort to build a computer model, based on the probabilistic
mobilization time and evacuation network, to estimate the time needed
for an evacuation event since 1986. Pidd, et al. [56] developed a pro­
totype spatial decision support system, where a geographical informa­
tion system was integrated with an object-oriented micro-simulator to
perform the population evacuation simulation. Chen, et al. [6] proposed
a simulation model considering factors, such as evacuee behavior and
traffic congestion, to evaluate the related evacuation risks. Cristiani and
Peri [10] employed simulation methods to investigate the role of ob­
stacles in evacuation events. It was found that the evacuation time could
be reduced if the obstacles can be optimally placed in the walking area.
Besides, a lot of studies have demonstrated that simulations could
qualitatively and quantitatively reproduce the evacuation process of
pedestrians, and the strategies and lessons from simulations could be
very helpful and provide suggestions to improve the evacuation in the
real situation [18,40].
The impacts of human behaviors on evacuation efficiency have been
extensively investigated in the literature. For instance, Aghabayk, et al.

and route choices on the safe evacuation. Fahad, et al. [13] investigated
the evacuation strategies that could shorten the evacuation time for
communities under extreme storms or hurricanes. Khalilpourazari and
Pasandideh [29] built models for seeking evacuation plans that could
evacuate and rescue people trapped in flood disasters. Some researchers
focused on the evacuation route choices and optimization under
terrorist attack situations [36,44,47]. Despite the different scenarios
investigated, common points could be found in these studies. Behavioral
characteristics of evacuees, evacuation route choice, the minimum time
required for the evacuation, and evacuation capacity were the key
subjects studied in those studies.

knowledge significantly impacted the evacuation performance of pas­
sengers in metro stations.
Reviewing these studies, it is not surprising that under different
scenarios, shortening the evacuation time, lowering the density, and
reducing losses are regarded as the objectives to improve the evacuation
in most of the studies. But it should be noticed that how to achieve these
common objectives could be widely divergent. Evacuation route choice
may not be as important as the awareness and training (how to transport
patients under critical conditions) for effective evacuation in hospitals,
but it could be the most significant factor for the residents' evacuation
safety in large communities. By analyzing the conditions on the partic­
ular scenario and providing suggestions based on the analysis, case-by-
case investigations could be a crucial process for the successful evacu­
ation assessment and optimization. Besides, compared to other places,
evacuation in metro stations owns its particular characteristics. Unlike
other spacious places or buildings, most of the stations are underground
and the station space is often long and narrow. The density in terms of
the number of passengers in the rail transit system is often much higher,
compared to ground transportation systems. The available space for
people to move around is relatively limited, and the passenger behavior
could be unpredictable under pressure. If something unexpected hap­
pens, it will cause more serious panic and confusion among passengers.
Another challenge in the metro station evacuation is that the occurrence
of different kinds of accidents would greatly affect how the passengers
should be safely evacuated. For example, an emergency evacuation due
to a fire disaster would be much tenser than the one due to train faults.
The requirements for the evacuation time and routes would be different.
These challenges bring difficulties to the improvement of the evacuation
at metro stations.
Besides, as discussed above, the evacuation improvement for metro
station scenarios should be treated as a MOO problem, due to complex
and even conflicting relationships between the potential objectives.
However, as presented in Table 1, most of the current studies still focus
on the improvement of the metro station evacuation from a single spe­
cific aspect, such as particularly focusing on reducing the evacuation
time, the management of firefighting facilities, how to use the elevator
for the evacuation or investigating the passenger behavior pattern to
renovate the metro station [34,45,51,61]. To fill the gap, this research
proposes a hybrid approach that could simulate the evacuation process
of metro stations, build the meta-model between influential factors and
objectives, and search the renovation solutions for the evacuation
problem at metro stations from the MOO perspective.
3. Methodology
To effectively evaluate the egress system of metro stations and ach­
ieve the optimization for a safe evacuation, a hybrid approach inte­
grating simulation, RF, and Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm
III (NSGA-III) is proposed in this research. Fig. 1 presents the workflow
of the proposed approach. Firstly, a detailed analysis of the metro station
evacuation is conducted, and an evaluation system is constructed based
on the identification of key influential factors. Secondly, the metro
station model is constructed, and the evacuation events are simulated
under different scenarios. A meta-model between the influential factors
and the evacuation objectives is built based on simulations, and a
sensitivity analysis is conducted. At last, together with the decision
rules, NSGA-III is employed to perform the multi-objective optimization.
3.1. Metro station evacuation analysis
The evacuation events under different scenarios could be disparate
due to the environmental characteristics. Different influential factors
should be considered especially based on different evacuation events.
The evacuation in metro stations has its own features. The path in metro
stations is often long and narrow, the density of passenger flow could be
extremely high, especially in the peak hours, and this brings a great
challenge to safely evacuate all the passengers within the very limited
time in metro stations. Three objectives, including the evacuation time,
density, and cost, are determined as the criteria for the evacuation
evaluation and optimization.
(1) Evacuation time. Evacuation time is determined as one objective
for the evacuation evaluation. People tend to show maladaptive
and relentless behaviors, such as jamming or overcrowding that
could even be life-threatening, under panic when an emergency
happens [76]. This indicates that a shorter time of the evacuation
could reduce the possible risks. Otherwise, a vicious circle could
be produced if the evacuation cannot be completed timely, where
the panic causes the damage which further intensifies the panic.
Given a metro station, the pedestrians will start evacuating as the
emergency alarm is issued, and the evacuation is considered
complete only when all the pedestrians are evacuated success­
fully from the main exit gates of the station.
(2) Density. Due to the high density and narrow space, a high pres­
sure is particularly easy to be produced in the crowds during the
evacuation at metro stations. Under pressure, the passenger
behavior could become even more unpredictable, and it could
cause unexpected events, leading to serious damages. Thus, the
density level during the evacuation is regarded as an objective for
the evacuation evaluation. Given a metro station, the density of
the passenger evacuation flow is measured at bottlenecks of the
station, where large crowds are likely to gather, such as the exits
and emergency exits, stairs, the routes that all evacuees have to
pass, and other turning points. In this research, the density is
measured with the built-in elements of the density map and
pedestrian statistics in Anylogic. The density map can present the
density levels of all passenger flows from an overall perspective,
and the pedestrian statistics tool can let users collect the density
data at any particular place. The maximum value of the density
levels (indicating the highest potential of causing risks) during
the evacuation process is adopted as the evaluation index.
(3) Cost. Cost is set as a criterion in almost every study [3,9,11,69].
Especially, metro stations are often constructed in the central
parts of cities, where a huge expenditure might be needed for the
renovation. Hence, the cost issue should be one of the objectives
considered in evacuation optimization.
Different features exist between different metro stations. For
example, a relatively larger space is allowed for the construction and

renovation of the metro stations in the suburbs, and even the station
expansion can be realized to accommodate a higher capacity of pas­
sengers. For the metro stations in the center of cities, a massive re-
construction may not be feasible and only internal structures could be
adjusted, such as the number and width of fare gates. Thus, by investi­
gating the site of the target metro station and discussing the key influ­
ential factors with the experts, the evacuees' behavior, the station
structure, and the guidance under the emergency are regarded as the
most important three aspects influencing the success of the evacuation.
(1) Evacuee behaviors. One of the particular features at the metro
station is that a highly dense number of passengers (passenger
volume x1) often exists [23]. It naturally becomes one of the most
critical factors influencing the evacuation. For the features of the
passengers, the passenger volume is obviously one of the most
important factors, and it is directly related to the evacuation time
and density. The average walking speed (x2) of the passengers is
set as another influential factor for the evacuee in metro stations,
which is directly related to the required time during the evacu­
ation process. Another important feature of the passengers is the
proportion of the herding behavior (x3) of passengers (the per­
centage of passengers who tend to move together) during the
evacuation events. Under emergency and pressure, people tend to
blindly follow the crowd flow without a clear judgment. Espe­
cially under the metro station scenarios where the space is nar­
row and the vision could be very limited, panic could be produced
during the evacuation and it breeds the herding behavior [66].
Furthermore, the herding behavior could push the crowd to
eventually move to the same jammed exits, leading to injures.
Therefore, the proportion of herding behavior is set as one
influential factor for the evacuation evaluation and optimization.
Certainly, a great diversity of people could exist in the passenger
groups, female and male, children and elderly, and even people
with disabilities. Stability and balance of the crowds could be
reached, especially during the peak hours, i.e., the composition of
different people is relatively stable [28]. Besides, the investiga­
tion of the evacuation evaluation and optimization mainly fo­
cuses on the evacuation conditions during the peak hours, the
passengers could be considered as a whole, and other features,
such as the gender and age distributions, are not included.
(2) Station structure. The station structure is a critical aspect of safe
evacuation. Many factors related to the station condition should
be considered. For a station constructed in the center of the city,
where land is an extremely valuable resource, construction
extension is nearly impossible. Thus, the evaluation and optimi­
zation of the station for the safe evacuation focus on the ratio­
nality of its internal structure. Thus, three sub-factors, the
number of fare gates (x4), the number of exits (x5), and obstacles
(x6) are considered as the influential factors in this research. Fare
gates are used as the necessary passage for passengers to leave the
station, and the number of fare gates may exert a direct influence
on the effectiveness of the evacuation [57]. Exits obviously can
help a lot with the evacuation, where more exits could efficiently
reduce the evacuation time [80]. The existence of obstacles is
another factor considered in this research. Different kinds of
obstacles in the metro station, such as the cleaning machines,
service desks, advertising boards, often exist, and obstacles play
an important role in interacting with pedestrians during evacu­
ation (the cleaning machine could keep the floors clean but could
hamper the evacuation due to its existence) [10].
(3) Evacuation guidance. As to the evacuation guidance, three sub-
factors are added into the evaluation system, i.e., the effective­
ness of signages (x7), the position of the ushers (x8), and the
number of ushers (x9). The effectiveness of the signages in the
stations is directly related to the utilization rate of all the normal
exits and emergency exits, which is could be decisive to the
success of evacuation events [14]. During the emergency evacu­
ation, pedestrian counterflows could happen because of panics,
and more panics and accidents could be triggered by the coun­
terflows. The proper evacuation guidance by emergency ushers is
especially important [24]. The ushers should play a critical role in
the evacuation events, the number of ushers is a factor that
should not be ignored [5].
With the consideration of the metro station features, an index system
is constructed for the evacuation evaluation and optimization, as pre­
sented in Fig. 2. Three objectives, including the evacuation time, den­
sity, and cost, are determined as the criteria for the evacuation
evaluation and optimization. Three aspects (i.e., the evacuee, station
structure, and emergency guidance) and nine second-level factors in
total are set as influential factors contributing to the success of evacu­
ation. Table 2 gives detailed descriptions of the influential factors and
objectives.

3.2. Evacuation simulation and meta-model construct
3.2.1. Simulation model for the evacuation evaluation
Anylogic is a windows-based development tool, which is often used
to create a professional virtual prototyping environment. It can also be
used for the simulations of discrete, continuous or mixed behavior of
complex systems. In the Anylogic simulation engine, a code generator
and graphical model could map the model into Java codes. The built
model in Anylogic is running on a Java platform, an interface can be
used to control the model execution, and the required information can
be retrieved from the text-based protocol over TCP/IP. System simula­
tion models, including virtual prototyping, the external environment,
physical equipment, and operating personnel, can be quickly built in
Anylogic. It has been proved as a powerful and flexible tool for simu­
lations in many different fields, including control systems, traffic,
manufacturing, supply lines, machinery, sewage treatment, logistics,
and others [32]. Due to its wide adaptation in both academia and in­
dustry, Anylogic is adopted in this research to build the evacuation
simulation in metro stations.
A pedestrian library in Anylogic is specially used to simulate the
physical environment of crowded people. Built-in functions can be used
to calculate the efficiency of the loads for the service points or to collect
data such as the density of pedestrian flows in different areas. The
pedestrian library can provide an advanced user interface, which allows
users to quickly build the flow-process diagrams. In addition, a rail li­
brary in Anylogic can let users build various railway models and visu­
alize them. Discrete events and agents can be included in the rail models,
in order to simulate the loading and unloading of passengers, allocating
resources, and other transport activities. Besides, users can also build
databases and flow-process diagrams according to particular re­
quirements. Fig. 3 presents an example of the simulation model con­

3.2.2. Meta-model construct
As analyzed above, one of the challenges in the evacuation optimi­
zation tasks is the elusive relationship between the influential factors
and evacuation objectives. The rapid development of computer-based
simulation and machine learning algorithms makes this challenging
task possible. A handful of methods can be used to construct the meta-
model to represent the factor and objective relationship. Methods
including kriging, splines, support vector machines (SVMs), Bayesian
network (BN), random forest (RF), and artificial neural networks (ANNs)
are the most commonly used methods for constructing meta-models
[78]. These methods possess their own features, and some of the
shortcomings set limitations for their applicability. For example, a low
efficiency may be presented in the spline and kriging meta-models,
especially for performing the simulations of complex projects with
high uncertainty. SVM and BN could be time-consuming, and ANNs are
often criticized for the heavy training process [49,74]. Comparatively,
owing to the capacity of constructing the complex nonlinear relation­

assumptions, RF possesses the advantage in solving complex engineering
problems [59]. Besides, it is demonstrated in studies that the applica­
tions of RF present other features, including a higher prediction accu­
racy and better feature selection.

4. Case study
Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) is a rail transit system in Singapore, which
is first constructed in 1987 and now covering the vast majority of the
city. Despite having one of the most developed railway networks, the
rapidly increasing ridership is forcing the government to upgrade the
metro systems in a continuous manner. Before the circuit breaker for
curbing the COVID-19, the average daily ridership in Singapore in 2019
reached 3.4 million. Due to the growing and development demand in
Singapore, the investigation for evacuation in the MRT system becomes
an indispensable task, since it is closely related to safety issues. Thus,
this research chooses one of the metro stations in Singapore to explore
the evacuation evaluation and optimization.
4.1. Background
Jurong East (JE) MRT station was built as part of the MRT extension
to the west of the city in Singapore, which is an elevated MRT inter­
change station that connects the North-East line and East-West line in
Jurong East, Singapore. It is located at the heart of Jurong Lake District,
with the surroundings of many shopping malls, bus interchanges, and
hospitals. The station has two levels, where Level 1 is the concourse level
and Level 2 is with three platforms for the interchange of four train lines.
Along with the rapidly increasing population, the great number of pas­
sengers, especially during the peak hours, has made the station more
crowded than it can seemly cope with. During peak hours, the station
has more than 20 thousand ridership per hour, and sometimes, it could
cost ten minutes for passengers to wait on the platform, passengers are
often queueing at the edge of the other platform [46]. This MRT station
was not designed for such a densely large population, and a high and
even extremely high passenger volume now exists in the station. This
indicates the necessity and urgency of evaluating the safety of the
evacuation events with the high passenger volume and optimizing it if
necessary.
Through the field investigation, features related to the evacuation in
the MRT station are noticed. As presented in Fig. 5 (b), the waiting
passengers are fully packed during peak hours. As shown in Fig. 5 (c)
and (d), some information boards, advertising boards, and service desks
are in the station, which could become obstacles in the evacuation
events. The same applies to the barricade in Fig. 5 (e), which could serve
as the railing diverting passengers in normal circumstances, but its effect
on the evacuation needs to be tested. Another problem is that there are
barely any signages for the emergency exits. As presented in Fig. 5 (f),
the emergency exit is at the farthest corner of the platform, but no
signages are observed in the station. Besides, due to the very limited
space, the escalators and stairs in the station have a very narrow width
(1 m and 1.5 m, respectively), as presented in Fig. 5 (g). Particularly,
there are three platforms in the station, but only one platform is
equipped with emergency exits at both ends, and there is only one
emergency exit for the other two platforms.

6. Conclusions and future works
Evacuation is a crucial part of the safety management at metro sta­
tions. This research proposes a hybrid approach, incorporating the
simulation tool, RF, and NSGA-III, to evaluate and optimize the evacu­
ation events at metro stations. A 3D model of the metro station is built
for the evacuation process simulation, and a detailed analysis is con­
ducted to identify the key influential factors and objectives for safe
evacuation. An RF-based meta-model is used to construct the relation­
ship between influential factors and objectives. NSGA-III is employed to
seeking the optimal solutions for the station renovation in order to
achieve a safe evacuation. The proposed approach in this research could
be expected to contribute to the safe evacuation management at metro
stations, by incorporating meta-model to identify the complex rela­
tionship between factors and objectives and effectively providing opti­
mization plans to promote the success of the evacuation from the MOO
perspective.
A case study simulating a real metro station in Singapore is con­
ducted to test the effectiveness of the proposed approach. It is found that
(1) A safe evacuation can be achieved in the metro station, but the
evacuation may not be able to meet the standard when the passenger
volume and panic levels are increasing. Especially under a high pas­
senger volume and panic scenario, the passenger density could reach up
to 6.2 unit/m2, which is an extremely dangerous level with the potential
of leading to serious consequences; (2) The proposed approach could
effectively provide effective renovation methods to achieve the evacu­
ation optimization. Especially for high passenger volume scenario, a
maximum 27.2% improvement degree could be achieved; (3) It could be
difficult to guarantee both the evacuation time and density within the
standards if one major exit is closed, but a larger average improvement
degree, 10.8%, can be achieved by the proposed optimization approach.
The results demonstrate the applicability and effectiveness of the pro­
posed approach. With the integration of simulation, RF-based meta-
model, and NSGA-III, the proposed hybrid approach can effectively
evaluate the evacuation and provide the optimal trade-off solutions
improving the evacuation events at metro stations.
However, limitations exist in this research. Currently, this research
focuses on the evacuation capacity of the metro station and the possible
renovation methods that could optimize the evacuation capacity to a
great extent under both normal conditions and special conditions when
one exit is closed. It has not been considered that how special events,
such as fire disasters, floods, or terrorist attacks, would affect evacuation
efficiency. For example, due to the fire hazard, the rapidly increased air
temperature and smoke density, and the decreased visibility could exert
a significant impact on the evacuation [39]. In addition, the uncertainty
in data monitoring and measurement (e.g., evacuee's behaviors) is
another significant factor that affects the quality of MOO [82].Those
would bring a great challenge for the evacuation management issue at
metro stations. Our future works aim to develop a more advanced
approach that is able to simulate and optimize the evacuation of metro
stations with the consideration of the influence of particular hazardous
events and uncertainties.
